title: Diurnal Intervention Effects of Electric Lighting on Alertness, Cognition, and Mood in Healthy Individuals: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
review_question: 1) Does diurnal electric lighting (DEL) intervention effectively improve human alertness, cognitive functions, and mood? 2) What is the relationship between the diurnal non-image forming (NIF) effects and light intervention attributes?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: healthy adults (18-60 years), RCTs/CBAs/CCTs (crossover/parallel-group), artificial lighting during daytime working period with control, English language, published before Dec 2022, psychological/cognitive/physiological measures used. Excluded: reviews without quantitative assessment, heterogeneous populations (clinical illness, irregular sleep-wake cycles, shift workers), dynamic light interventions, non-acute NIF effects (circadian), missing means/SDs.

synthesis_conclusions: Diurnal electric lighting (DEL) intervention significantly improved subjective and objective alertness.
DEL intervention had cognitive-enhancement effects, particularly with short-wavelength light and morning exposure.
DEL intervention can activate arousal levels by inhibiting EEG alpha wave.
DEL intervention had no significant effects on subjective mood (positive or negative).
The diurnal NIF effects of DEL depended largely on the coupling induction of light parameters, timing, and duration of exposure.
evidence_gaps: Further investigation into the correlation between light parameters and time characteristics on human responses.
Need for larger sample sizes to clarify the regulatory role of light intervention duration on cognitive performance.
Further research on the potential regulatory effects of chronotypes in diurnal NIF effects.
More efficient approaches of EEG analysis to characterize neurobehavioral dynamics with more precise time and spatial resolution.
Investigation of modulations of task heterogeneity on human photobiological response, requiring new tasks particularly sensitive to DEL intervention.
More in-depth analysis of social and cultural factors and individual characteristics in emotional lighting studies.
Extensive research needed to draw concrete conclusions due to sparse data in some subgroups.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Quality Assessment Tool for Quantitative Studies (EPHPP) used. Most studies had 'moderate' to 'strong' global ratings. High risk of bias in blinding criteria (85% 'weak' due to open trials, 11% 'moderate' for not reporting awareness). 7% 'moderate' in withdrawals/drop-outs (60-79% completion).
heterogeneity_sources: High heterogeneity for negative mood (I²=67%) and PVT Reaction Time (I²=76%).
Study characteristics (e.g., chronotype of participants) contributed to differences in RT-based meta-analysis.
Insufficient evidence to study time domain, frequency domain, and time-frequency domain characteristics of EEG related to neurobehavior mechanisms.
Task heterogeneity (differences in paradigms characterizing cognitive functions) may play a potential regulatory role in diurnal NIF effects.
publication_bias: Likely publication bias for cognitive performance (RT) based on funnel plot inspection, Begg's test (z= -2.10, p = .04), and Egger's test (t = -2.59, df = 9, p = .03). No significant publication bias for subjective alertness.

moderators.effect: Bright light (≥1000 lx) significantly improved subjective alertness, but cold or short-wavelength light did not. Short-wavelength light (Amax ≤ 480 nm) significantly improved cognitive performance, but bright or cold light did not.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Subjective alertness: Bright light (SMD = -0.25, p = .004). Cognitive performance: Short-wavelength light (SMD = -0.42, p = .005).

moderators.effect: Both morning and afternoon DEL interventions significantly improved subjective alertness. Morning intervention showed a medium significant effect size for cognitive performance, but afternoon intervention did not.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Subjective alertness: Morning (SMD = -0.41, p = .006), Afternoon (SMD = -0.18, p = .05). Cognitive performance: Morning (SMD = -0.61, p = .005).

moderators.effect: Both short-term (<60 min) and long-term (≥60 min) DEL interventions significantly improved subjective alertness. Short-term intervention showed a small significant effect size for cognitive performance, but long-term intervention did not.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Subjective alertness: Short-term (SMD = -0.20, p = .02), Long-term (SMD = -0.26, p = .03). Cognitive performance: Short-term (SMD = -0.34, p = .01).

limitations: High risk of bias in blinding criteria (85% 'weak' scoring) may affect results, requiring cautious interpretation.
Limited data prevented detailed meta-analysis of individual factors (e.g., chronotype, gender, age, prior light history) and task attributes (e.g., cognitive domain, task difficulty).
Sparse data in some subgroups (e.g., CCT subgroup for subjective alertness) increased result variation and reduced power to detect actual effects.

theory_commitments.theory_name: Non-visual effects of light / Circadian photoreception
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Light exposure, particularly to blue wavelengths, activates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), influencing circadian rhythm, melatonin secretion, and direct neural pathways to alertness and mood centers, independent of image formation.

mechanism_chain.description: Electric lighting, especially with higher intensity and blue spectral content, activates ipRGCs in the retina. These cells project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) and other non-image-forming brain regions. This activation modulates circadian rhythm, suppresses melatonin production, and directly influences brain areas involved in arousal, attention, and mood regulation, leading to changes in alertness, cognitive performance, and mood.
